findings.claim: The model answer says the solera's 'mathematical average age climbs indefinitely', and the accept list takes 'running wine down through the scales raises the average age indefinitely'.
findings.because: With a fixed fraction drawn each year, a solera's average age rises toward a limit (about 1 + K/α, where K is the number of scales and α the fraction moved) and levels off there. It does not keep rising. For example, a three-scale solera drawing a third a year settles at about five years.
findings.fix: ans: replace 'the mathematical average age climbs indefinitely' with 'the average age rises toward a stable equilibrium set by the number of scales and the fraction drawn'; accept: remove 'running wine down through the scales raises the average age indefinitely'
findings.verifyReason:
The finding holds. I opened the question, m-7uila2vu in batch-179.json. Its model answer says "the mathematical average age climbs indefinitely", and accept[2] takes "running wine down through the scales raises the average age indefinitely". Both are false. When a solera draws a fixed fraction each year and refreshes the top scale with new wine, the average age rises only toward an equilibrium and never passes it.

I checked this by working the system out as a steady state. A single scale drawing a fraction f each year settles where A = (1-f)(A+1), so A = (1-f)/f. With K scales, the average age at steady state is roughly K divided by the fraction drawn, plus one, depending on when in the year you measure. That is a limit, not unbounded growth.

Wikipedia's Solera article, which I opened, says the same: the average age "asymptotically approaches ... (1 + K/α)" and "asymptotically converges on five years as the solera continues". The traces of very old vintages never disappear, but they shrink exponentially and do not keep raising the mean. Cycling wine through the scales produces a stable average, not an ever-rising one.

One caution: the examiner's worked example, a three-scale solera drawing a third a year settling at about five years, does not check out. By my calculation that setup settles nearer nine years, so the five-year figure must come from a different setup. The fix does not use that number, so it still stands. It removes a false statement and a false accept entry. The other three accept entries still let a correct answer through.

Outside this finding: the stem's premise that a sherry's "average age can exceed the age of any barrel in it", and accept[0], look questionable and may deserve their own review.
findings.finalFix: ans: replace "the mathematical average age climbs indefinitely" with "the average age rises toward a stable equilibrium set by the number of scales and the fraction drawn"; accept: remove "running wine down through the scales raises the average age indefinitely"

question.q: Explain the criaderas y solera system, and why a sherry's average age can exceed the age of any barrel in it.
accept: fractional blending through scales so the average age exceeds any single barrel
solera and criaderas refreshed in sequence by saca and rocio
running wine down through the scales raises the average age indefinitely
nothing is ever emptied so a trace of every vintage remains
question.ans: The wine is held in scales: the solera on the floor, the criaderas stacked above it in order of increasing youth. Wine for sale is drawn from the solera — the saca, and only a fraction of each butt is taken — that scale is topped up from the first criadera, which is topped up from the second, and so on to the youngest scale, which receives the new vintage, the rocío. Nothing is ever emptied, so every butt retains an exponentially decaying trace of every year that has ever entered it: the mathematical average age climbs indefinitely, while no barrel anywhere in the system holds unblended old wine. That fractional blending has three purposes — it erases vintage variation so the house style is reproducible, it keeps biological wines supplied with the fresh nutrients flor needs to survive, and it lets a small stock of very old wine season a much larger volume. Jerez requires a minimum of two years' ageing.
question.exp: Two consequences to have ready: flor is a living organism that starves without refreshment, which is the practical reason finos are run so often; and consistency, not age, is the system's original commercial purpose — it was built to satisfy a shipping trade that wanted the same wine every year.

question.q: Explain what the recent reform of the Jerez DO changed.
accept: the ageing zone was widened unfortified wines allowed and old varieties restored
the triangle was opened up and vino de pasto was legalised
recognised unfortified pasto wines vineyard pago names and historic grapes
brought vineyard identity vintage and old varieties back into the do
question.ans: It reopened the region to its own history. The ageing zone had been confined to Jerez de la Frontera, El Puerto de Santa María and Sanlúcar — the famous triangle — and was extended across the wider production zone, so towns like Trebujena, Chipiona, Chiclana and Rota that had always grown grapes may now age wine under the DO. Unfortified wines were recognised, which legitimised the vino de pasto movement that had been forced to sell its Palomino as table wine outside the appellation. Single-vineyard pago names and vintage-dated wines may now be labelled. And historic varieties beyond Palomino, Pedro Ximénez and Moscatel — among them Beba, Perruno, Vejeriego, Cañocazo and the Mantúos — were restored to the permitted list. Taken together it converts a set of rules describing a 20th-century shipping business into rules describing a place.
question.exp: The trade-off is real: the DO gives up some brand control — a guarantee that sherry means fortified wine aged in three specific towns — in exchange for terroir language it needs to compete for attention. Equipo Navazos, Luis Pérez and Muchada-Léclapart had already proved the market existed outside the rules.

question.q: Make the case for Montilla-Moriles as something more than a cheaper Jerez.
accept: pedro ximenez based unfortified generosos aged in tinajas in cordoba
px ripens to fifteen percent so fortification is unnecessary
inland cordoba making unfortified finos and the greatest px
same solera system but px instead of palomino and no fortification
question.ans: It lies inland in Córdoba, hotter and far more continental than the coast, with albariza in its best sites — the Sierra de Montilla and Moriles Alto. Its grape is Pedro Ximénez, not Palomino, and it ripens to such sugar that the base wines reach around fifteen per cent alcohol naturally, so its generosos — fino, amontillado, oloroso — are traditionally made with no fortification at all, which is legally impossible in Jerez. It ferments in tinajas, the tall earthenware jars, it runs the same criaderas y solera system, and it makes the greatest Pedro Ximénez in Spain, having supplied Jerez with sweetening wine for generations. What it lacks is the Atlantic: without Sanlúcar's humidity and cool the flor grows thinner, so the finos are broader, nuttier and shorter-lived under flor than a manzanilla.
question.exp: The unfortified generoso is the real point of difference and the easiest sell on a list: a fino that never saw spirit. Know also that the historic export of Montilla PX into Jerez has been progressively closed off, which is part of why the region now argues its own case.

Cantemerle was added in 1856, and Mouton Rothschild was promoted from Second to First Growth in 1973, the best-known fact about the classification. The Sauternes list itself has changed through subdivisions: 9 original Premiers Crus are now 11, and 11 original Deuxièmes are now 15. The answer admits this in its own opening sentence. A candidate who says 'unchanged since 1855' in an oral will be corrected.

question.q: Set out the 1855 Sauternes classification and explain the Barsac wrinkle.
accept: yquem alone as premier cru superieur then eleven firsts and fifteen seconds unchanged since 1855
one superior first growth then first and second growths from 1855
barsac estates may label as barsac or sauternes
climens and coutet are classified barsac properties
question.ans: One Premier Cru Supérieur standing alone — Château d'Yquem — then, after a century and a half of divisions among the original properties, eleven Premiers Crus, including Climens, Coutet, Suduiraut, Guiraud, Rieussec, La Tour Blanche, Lafaurie-Peyraguey, Clos Haut-Peyraguey, Rabaud-Promis, Sigalas-Rabaud and Rayne Vigneau, and fifteen Deuxièmes Crus. It was drawn up alongside the Médoc reds for the 1855 Exposition, on the basis of the prices the wines had been fetching, and like the Médoc list it stands today exactly as drawn. The wrinkle: Barsac is one of the five communes entitled to the Sauternes appellation but also holds its own, so a Barsac estate may label its wine either Barsac or Sauternes as it chooses. Climens and Coutet are classified properties sitting in Barsac, on flatter ground with more limestone beneath, which is the usual explanation for Barsac's comparatively lighter, more incisive style.
question.exp: Sweet Bordeaux is classified territory and the structure is examinable in itself; the Barsac dual-labelling right is the part candidates fumble. Be ready to add that the classification is a price list from 1855 and predicts quality today only loosely — Yquem's position, however, has stood unchallenged throughout.

findings.claim: The model answer says that besides tartaric, "malic, lactic and citric are also permitted" for acidification, with citric held to 1 g/L. The explanation adds that lactic acid "barely moves pH at all".
findings.because: Under Annex VIII Part I Section C of Reg. (EU) 1308/2013, supplemented by Reg. (EU) 2019/934, three acids are authorised for acidifying musts and wines: L(+) tartaric, malic (L or DL) and DL-lactic. Citric acid is not an acidifying agent under EU law. Its 1 g/L ceiling is a limit on its use as a stabiliser (against iron casse). The same Laffort regulatory sheet gives the maximum dose as 4 g/L as tartaric (53.3 meq/L), which agrees with the answer, and it rates lactic's effect on pH (++) the same as malic's, below tartaric (+++). So lactic does move pH, only less efficiently than tartaric. A student who names citric as an EU acidifier would be marked wrong. The answer's zone split (A and B deacidify, C acidifies) comes from the pre-2021 text, and the 4 g/L single ceiling it quotes comes from the later amended text. That point is left for separate checking because the amended EUR-Lex text could not be opened.

https://www.legislation.gov.uk/eur/2013/1308/annex/VIII/2013-12-17 (original Annex VIII Part I Section C, with zones and limits)

Tartaric acid L(+), malic acid (D,L and L) and lactic acid are the only acids there; the rest are potassium tartrate, potassium bicarbonate, calcium carbonate, calcium tartrate, calcium sulphate and potassium carbonate. It is still an authorised acidifier and does lower pH, so 'barely moves pH at all' overstates the case. question.q: Explain acidification and deacidification: the materials used, and how EU law rations them by wine zone.
accept: tartaric acid up to 4 g/l calcium carbonate to deacidify the north enriches the south acidifies
add tartaric acid in warm zones deacidify in cool zones and enrichment excludes acidification in the same wine
enrichment and acidification of the same wine are forbidden
the eu wine zones decide who may chaptalize and who may acidify
zone a to zone c ladder with tartaric acid as the acidifier
question.ans: Acidification normally means adding tartaric acid — malic, lactic and citric are also permitted, citric constrained by a 1 g/L ceiling in the finished wine — up to a maximum of 4 g/L expressed as tartaric. Deacidification removes acid with calcium carbonate, potassium bicarbonate or potassium tartrate, capped at 1 g/L expressed as tartaric. The EU divides its vineyard into zones A through C: the cool north (A and B) gets the largest enrichment allowances and may deacidify, while the warm south (Zone C) may acidify — with exceptional-year derogations now blurring both edges. The governing principle is that enrichment and acidification of the same product are mutually exclusive: you may not add sugar and acid to the same wine.
question.exp: Two things to say aloud. First the arithmetic of the ladder — enrichment ceilings fall as you go south, roughly 3% potential alcohol in Zone A, 2% in B and 1.5% in Zone C, because the law was written for a 1970s climate and assumed the south had sugar to spare. That assumption is what warming has broken, hence the pressure for acidification derogations in Zone B. Second, why tartaric is the acid of choice: it is the grape's own acid, microbially stable, and lowers pH efficiently, whereas malic feeds spoilage bacteria unless malolactic conversion is completed, and lactic barely moves pH at all.
